newsitem.title: USA: US claims data surprise, hint at strong labor mkt.
newsitem.headline: US claims data surprise, hint at strong labor mkt.

text.p: The number of jobless claims filed in the week ended August 31 fell short of expectations, supporting the case for a strong labor market one day prior to the release of pivotal August U.S. payrolls, analysts said.
U.S. cash Treasuries and debt futures dropped sharply on news claims fell 15,000 to 316,000 compared to consensus forecasts for a 4,000 rise to 335,000. Claims tallied 331,000 in the prior week.
"When I see a number like this for claims, it makes me feel happier about the high side of my payroll estimate range," said Peter Kretzmer, economist at NationsBank Corp.
Economists were quick to note the survey week for the August payrolls, the week containing the 12th, fell well before Thursday's jobless claims for the week ended August 31.

"Every week claims don't pop up to the old 350,000 or so level is an indication that this is more than seasonal adjustment problems and the labor market is actually stronger than one might have expected," Kretzmer said.

Kretzmer predicts August U.S. payrolls, scheduled for release 0830 EDT/1230 GTM on Friday, will fall between 240,000 to 270,000. The consensus forecast in a Reuters poll is for a 244,000 August gain, compared to 193,000 in July.
The lower-than-expected claims data surprised many money market participants, triggering a sell-off that brought the benchmark 30-year bond down by more than half a point.
"Basically what (the jobless claims report) does is sort of remind everyone of the risk going into the employment (numbers) tomorrow," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at CS First Boston.

"It surprised the market for sure, but it's not any lower than what we've seen over the last couple of weeks," Alexy added. Shortly after the data was released, the benchmark T-bond was off 17/32 at 95-4/32 yielding 7.15 percent.
Some economists were hesitant to read too much into the typically volatile claims report.

"It does suggest a healthy labor market, but doesn't necessarily suggest greater payrolls than what's already expected," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International, who has forecast a 225,000 rise in August payrolls.
